title: Coupling phase interference effects in a multimode cavity magnonics system
authors: M. Avicena, G. Bourcin, V. Vlaminck, J. Bourhill, V. Castel
abstract: Coupling phases play a decisive yet often overlooked role in cavity magnonics, particularly in complex multimode systems. Here, we investigate phase-mediated interference effects in a cavity magnonics system comprising a four-post re-entrant microwave cavity coupled to Yttrium Iron Garnet (YIG) spheres. Using an input-output model that explicitly accounts for both internal and external coupling phases, we achieve agreement with experimental microwave transmission measurements. Our results unravel the emergence of a positionally-dependent uncoupled mode due to interference of cavity photon-magnon (internal) coupling phases. Further, we experimentally observed large nonreciprocity at the antiresonance frequencies and show that this feature arises due to the far-detuned modes' odd parity cavity photon-probe (external) coupling phase interfering with the internal coupling phases. Bridging theory, simulation and experiment, these results establish coupling-phase engineering as a key principle for accurately modeling and designing multimode cavity magnonics devices.
summary: This paper investigates how coupling phase interference dictates behavior in complex multimode cavity magnonics systems using YIG spheres. By developing an advanced input-output model that accounts for both internal and external phases, the authors successfully explain observed phenomena like nonreciprocity. The work establishes 'coupling-phase engineering' as a vital design principle for future quantum microwave devices.
main_problem: The study investigates how coupling phases critically influence interference effects within complex, multimode cavity magnonics systems.
main_result: The research establishes that engineering these coupling phases is a key principle for accurately modeling and designing advanced cavity magnonics devices, explaining phenomena like position-dependent modes and nonreciprocity.
method: The authors employ an input-output model formalism, combining theoretical Hamiltonian analysis with extensive numerical simulations (COMSOL) and comparison against real microwave transmission measurements using a VNA.
model_or_system: The physical system is a cavity magnonics setup involving Yttrium Iron Garnet (YIG) spheres coupled to a four-post re-entrant microwave cavity. The model explicitly incorporates both internal coupling phases (from the magnon field overlap) and external coupling phases (related to far-detuned modes).
key_observables: Transmission ($S_{12}$) and isolation responses versus frequency and external magnetic field ($\mu_0H$); nonreciprocity at antiresonance frequencies.
important_parameters: Internal and external coupling phases ($	heta_{uv}, \varphi_{up}$), cavity/magnon resonance frequencies, and the strong-coupling regime leading to polaritons.
main_assumptions: The model extends prior work by explicitly including far-detuned modes, which is crucial for correctly predicting nonreciprocity. Simplifications include assuming zero crosstalk between ports in some calculations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the cavity geometry and experimental setup; simulations show magnetic field distributions (EF) and frequency sweeps of transmission spectra ($S_{12}$) compared to experiment.
paper_structure: The paper builds from defining the physical system and theoretical model using input-output formalism, detailing how internal and external coupling phases are incorporated. It then presents results demonstrating mode splitting, position dependence due to phase interference, and nonreciprocity arising from combined phase effects.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it treats magnon-photon interactions—a core topic in cavity QED/AMO physics—by focusing on the subtle role of quantum phases. The methodology of 'coupling-phase engineering' provides a powerful, generalizable tool for controlling light-matter interaction dynamics.
